Definition: Whether the system enables consumer payments to merchants and businesses for goods and services, including retail purchases, bill payments, e-commerce, and subscription services.
Comments: PayShap is expanding beyond P2P to person-to-business (P2B) through “PayShap Request” (request-to-pay) enabling individuals, businesses, and informal traders to request immediate payments, supporting merchant acceptance use cases ([Stitch](https://www.stitch.money/blog/how-south-africa-is-gearing-up-for-payshap-request-rtp)).  This indicates active development/rollout of P2B capability, though adoption is emerging rather than universal.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed, Value Code 2 (Yes). PayShap merchant/P2B payments have now actually launched via merchant-presented QR codes at point of sale (Payments Africa News; BankservAfrica statement, Mar 2025), moving beyond the request-to-pay pilot cited in the single original source. Two independent, dated sources corroborate.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: SARB’s Vision 2025 for the National Payment System explicitly includes financial inclusion objectives (e.g., broaden access and reduce reliance on cash) and references collaborative governance with industry bodies like PASA/BankservAfrica rather than a dedicated pro-poor governance body ([South African Reserve Bank – Vision 2025](https://www.resbank.co.za/en/home/what-we-do/national-payment-system/overview/vision-2025)).  This indicates inclusion is a formal objective, but governance mechanisms specific to pro-poor representation are limited/indirect.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed, Value Code 2 (Partial). PASA's Constitution lists 'inclusion' and consumer financial education among its formal objectives, but SARB's own 2018 PASA Review consultation paper documents non-bank exclusion from membership and inadequate representation of non-members/consumers on PASA's governing Council, i.e. inclusion is a stated aspiration rather than a guaranteed structural mechanism (e.g. no reserved consumer/SME seats).

Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: PayShap participation/product rules are not fully published as a single publicly accessible “scheme rulebook”; instead, consumer-facing rules and usage conditions are mainly available via bank-specific PayShap terms and conditions (e.g., Standard Bank PayShap T&Cs describing ShapID registration and transaction rules) ([Standard Bank](https://www.standardbank.co.za/southafrica/personal/products-and-services/digital-banking/ways-to-bank/standard-bank-app/payshap/terms-and-conditions)).  Public information about PayShap exists on SARB/BankservAfrica pages, but comprehensive scheme rules for all participants are not clearly available openly.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Changed from 2 (Partial - On Request) to 1 (No - Confidential). AfricaNenda's 2024 SIIPS PayShap case study states the PayShap scheme rules are 'shared on a need-to-know basis', and PayInc's own PFMI Disclosure Framework confirms its governance policies (which include the Scheme Rules) 'are not generally available for public consumption', limited to onboarded participants rather than obtainable simply 'on request'. The original single source (a bank's consumer T&Cs) addressed customer terms, not participant scheme-rule availability, so did not actually support the stated score.

Definition: Percentage of the adult population (15+ years) who have made at least one digital payment transaction through the instant payment system in the past 90 days, indicating active usage rather than just account ownership.
Comments: The World Bank Global Findex database reports a high level of account ownership in South Africa (proxy for potential active digital payment user base), supporting a strong foundation for digital payments usage ([World Bank Global Findex](https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/globalfindex)).  Publicly available summaries indicate around ~70%+ adults with an account, consistent with a large share of the population able to use digital payments.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Changed from 4 (70-89%) to 1 (<20%). The variable specifically measures active use of the instant payment system (PayShap) in the past 90 days; general Findex account-ownership figures are not a valid proxy for this and do not support the original score. TechCentral (May 2026) reports PayShap has passed only six million registered users out of roughly 45 million adults, and independent transaction analysis (ClearingPost, Mar 2026) found PayShap accounts for under 7% of debit transactions even at the bank with the highest customer adoption (Absa, 68% adoption). Registered users alone are well under 20% of the adult population, so 90-day active users must be lower still.

Definition: Whether independent external audits of payment system security, operations, financial controls, and compliance are conducted by third-party auditors, and whether audit results or summaries are made public.
Comments: SARB provides oversight and monitoring of the National Payment System and publishes NPS-related reports/communications consistent with regulatory reviews and supervisory transparency ([South African Reserve Bank – NPS](https://www.resbank.co.za/en/home/what-we-do/national-payment-system)).  PayShap is part of the regulated NPS environment, and operator reporting plus central bank oversight implies routine review, though explicit independent audit reports for PayShap itself are not widely published in public sources.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Not confirmed with full confidence; recommend human review. SARB's National Payment System Regulatory and Oversight Report 2024 (11th edition, published annually) documents independent regulatory assessment of BankservAfrica/PayInc's compliance with the PFMI as a designated systemically important FMI, and PayInc's own PFMI Disclosure Framework describes a rolling internal audit programme plus an annual public Business Review. This is a plausible fit for Public Audits (3), but it is PFMI/regulatory compliance review rather than a classic independent third-party financial or security audit, so the fit to this variable's definition is imperfect — flagging for human judgement rather than asserting outright confirmation.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: Refugees and asylum seekers in South Africa can access at least some government digital payment programs: UNHCR South Africa’s guidance on the SASSA SRD grant states eligibility includes “Refugee registered on the Home Affairs database” and “an asylum seeker whose section 22 permit… is valid,” and applicants can use a DHA refugee/asylum permit number, indicating documented access pathways with valid documentation ([UNHCR South Africa](https://help.unhcr.org/southafrica/2022/02/21/sassa-srd-r350-grant/)).  However, access is tied to legal status and documentation, and broader payment inclusion for undocumented migrants is not clearly supported in official sources, suggesting partial inclusion.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed, Value Code 2 (Partial), with stronger and more direct sourcing than the original (which concerned a specific grant, not payment accounts generally). Financial Intelligence Centre guidance (PCC03/03A, PCC27) confirms refugees and asylum seekers with valid Home Affairs permits can open bank/digital payment accounts via an online DHA verification system, and major banks (e.g. Nedbank) offer dedicated refugee accounts. Access is nonetheless conditional on maintaining valid, renewed documentation (asylum permits valid only 6 months, refugee permits 24 months), and the FIC has had to intervene over banks freezing accounts on permit expiry — evidencing genuine but partial, documentation-dependent access rather than full inclusion.
